The kitchen was quiet, save for the rhythmic *thump-thump-thump* of the dough being kneaded on the floured wooden board. It was a primal sound, grounding and steady, a counterpoint to the chaotic storm raging in Clara’s chest.

"Flour," she whispered, her voice cracking slightly. "Water. Salt. Yeast."

She reached for the jar of coarse sea salt, her fingers trembling. The grains spilled over her thumb, sharp and cold, mirroring the ache in her ribs. She sprinkled them into the well she’d made in the center of the flour mound, watching the white crystals disappear into the pale dust. It was a simple alchemy, this turning of inert powders into something alive, something that rose and breathed.

She looked up, her gaze drifting past the window where the last embers of the sunset were fading into a bruised purple twilight. The ocean outside was no longer vibrant; it was a dark, heaving mass, swallowing the light just as grief had swallowed her father.

Clara’s hand drifted to her pocket, her fingers brushing the rough, frayed brim of the hat. She pulled it out, holding it up to the dim kitchen light. The fabric was worn thin at the crown, the brim bent from years of wear. She could almost smell him—tobacco and old paper and the faint, salty tang of the sea breeze he loved so much.

"Each fiber seems to carry a memory," she murmured, tracing the stitching with her thumb. A laugh echoed in her mind, bright and unburdened, from a summer day when the sun hadn't dipped below the horizon yet. A whisper of a song, a lullaby he used to hum while fixing the boat.

But then, the memory shifted. The laughter faded, replaced by the silence of the hospital room, the beep of the monitor slowing, the cold fingers of finality wrapping around her heart. The grief was a physical weight, pressing down on her shoulders, making the air in the kitchen feel thin and hard to breathe.

She looked back at the dough. It had begun to rise, slowly, imperceptibly, expanding against the confines of the bowl. It was stubborn. It was alive.
